newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Volatility play seen in OEX.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Volatility play seen in OEX.

text.p: Early volatility in U.S. stocks apparently enticed some investors to make a play for more volatility at the close, when August S&P 100 index .OEX options go off the board, analysts said Friday.
Most early volume in OEX options was in the August 890 call and put and the 895 call and in each case, the volume was greater than the option's open interest.

"It looks like they're setting up for little bit of a volatility play at the end of the day," Michael Schwartz, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co, said. "It looks like they're going to be net long the 890 straddle."
The trade may be profitable if the market rises or falls, if the investors went long the straddle.
"Somebody's taking a gamble," said Harrison Roth, a first vice president at Cowen & Co. "They might have been doing the straddle."
Schwartz said the market's early volatility was a good indication of more volatility at the close.
Stocks fell sharply in the first few minutes of trading, touching off downside limits in S&P 500 futures and trading curbs at the New York Stock Exchange.
The Dow industrial average .DJI fell nearly 125 points before recovering some ground. By about 1120 CDT/1620 GMT, it was down 86 points at 7,856.
September S&P 500 futures, meanwhile, were off 9.80 at 918.25 after hitting their initial 15-point downside limit in early action.
The OEX lost 8.83 to 888.33 and the spot S&P 500 .SPX fell 9.37 to 915.40.
The OEX August 890 call traded 14,165 contracts compared with its open interest of 5,800. The August 890 put traded about 11,890. It had open interest of 11,380 contracts.
The August 895 call traded 11,830 contracts and the August 900 call traded 10,435. Those two options had open interest of 4,532 and 10,671, respectively.

Schwartz said investors may have sold some of the August 895 calls to reduce the cost of the 890 straddle but it was still a fairly expensive trade, even if the prices were close to their theoretical value.

He added that OEX traders could be taking the other side of the trade anticipating "that the movement will not exceed the total sum of the premiums they're taking in and they're protecting themselves on the upside by buying some 895 calls."
Jerry Hegarty, an options analyst at Thomson Financial Services in Boston, said the heavy volume in the at- and near-the-money options was not surprising.
"Any time you're at the money, you're going to get some action," he said. "The only reason the outstanding (open) interest is so low is that a week ago they were 50 points in-the-money."
